title: Subacute ocular movements and gait instability with unrevealing initial tests
purpose: Represent the neurological syndrome despite unrevealing initial investigations.
decision_point: Reconstructed initial-admission review, before immunotherapy or follow-up. History, examination, initial MRI/CSF and standard antibody-panel findings are requestable. The tissue-based assay is deliberately withheld experimentally; the article includes it in the initial diagnostic work-up and does not establish a separate later date.
opening: A 60-year-old man has one month of progressively blurred vision, dizziness and gait instability with frequent abnormal eye movements.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Characterise the neurological syndrome, prioritise a differential and explain how the available negative tests affect diagnostic confidence and further assessment. After up to six question turns, provide a clinician-facing final assessment of 180–260 words. A precise final aetiology is not required. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
adaptation: Published clinical facts are paraphrased into fixed patient/record replies. Opening, task, six-turn limit, requirements and release rules are researcher-designed. The tissue-based assay occurred within the report's initial diagnostic work-up but is deliberately withheld for the experiment; this is not a claim that it occurred after standard tests or was unavailable to the real team. Later therapy and ten-month follow-up are excluded chronologically. No negative test, exposure, medication history or date is added beyond the source.
hidden: Weak serum neuronal tissue-assay reactivity with negative CSF tissue assay, the authors' initial diagnostic label, immunotherapy and response, later gastrointestinal symptoms, gastric cancer diagnosed ten months later, and follow-up outcomes. The later cancer and its unproven causal association are not initial diagnostic targets.

facts.text: Blurred vision, dizziness and walking difficulty have progressed over about a month. I have not had double vision, limb weakness or a febrile illness since this began.

The reported earlier medical history is unremarkable. There is no reported smoking, alcohol abuse or neurotoxin exposure, and no reported family history of autoimmune, neurological or neoplastic disease.

Admission vital signs and systemic examination were normal. There was continuous ocular flutter, a mild horizontal head/neck tremor, a broad-based gait and unsteadiness with eyes open or closed. Pupils and eye-movement range were normal; limb strength and pinprick/vibration sensation were preserved, reflexes were symmetric and Babinski signs absent.
Initial CSF opening pressure was normal, with white cells 12 × 10^6/L and normal protein, glucose and chloride. CSF pathogen mNGS was negative. Oligoclonal bands and the IgG index were not assessed.

High-resolution brain MRI with and without contrast showed no acute infarct, demyelination or structural brainstem/cerebellar lesion; the figure description also reports no abnormal contrast enhancement in those regions.

Routine peripheral blood tests, comprehensive metabolic panels and thyroid function were reported as unremarkable or normal. B lymphocytes were increased at 915/μL and 31.38% against the article's stated reference ranges; T-cell and NK-cell quantities were within those ranges.

The reported commercial fixed cell-based and immunoblot tests for established neural antibodies were negative, including the listed neuronal, demyelinating, onconeural and ganglioside targets. This statement concerns the standard specific-antibody panels; the tissue-based assay is outside this experimental packet.

At the initial presentation there were no reported weight-loss or gastrointestinal symptoms. Serum CEA, CA19-9 and AFP were within normal limits. Endoscopy and whole-body PET-CT were deferred; they were not negative investigations.

reference: Integrate the subacute ocular-motor and cerebellar findings into a provisional neurological syndrome. An unrevealing MRI and negative standard neural-antibody panels do not, by themselves, explain or exclude the clinically supported process. Mild CSF pleocytosis is supportive context rather than proof of a specific aetiology; negative pathogen testing and reported exposure/metabolic information should change the differential proportionately. Keep structural, infectious, immune-mediated, toxic/metabolic and other context-appropriate causes under consideration with defensible prioritisation. Normal tumour markers and deferred investigations do not establish comprehensive exclusion of malignancy. A specific tissue-assay result, final diagnostic label, future tumour or treatment response must not be demanded. Candidate requests and exact next investigations await clinical confirmation.

answer:
**Final Assessment**

This 60-year-old man presents with a subacute progressive cerebellar-brainstem syndrome: continuous ocular flutter, horizontal head tremor, and broad-based gait ataxia over one month, with preserved limb strength, sensation, and reflexes. The mild CSF pleocytosis with negative pathogen mNGS and a structurally normal brain MRI localise the process to a non-structural, likely immune-mediated aetiology.

Prioritised explanations:

1. Autoimmune or paraneoplastic encephalitis targeting the cerebellum or brainstem. The subacute course, ocular flutter, and gait ataxia are characteristic. The negative standard antibody panel reduces the probability of a known-antibody-mediated process but does not exclude it, as the tissue-based assay was not performed and novel antibodies may be present.

2. Occult malignancy with paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome. Tumor markers are normal, but whole-body PET-CT and endoscopy were deferred, so malignancy remains unexcluded.

3. Inflammatory or demyelinating process. MRI argues against classic demyelination, yet oligoclonal bands and IgG index were not assessed, leaving intrathecal immune activation uncharacterised.

Proportionate next steps: perform the tissue-based assay, assess oligoclonal bands and IgG index, complete tumour screening (PET-CT, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, age-appropriate screening), and consider empiric immunotherapy if clinical suspicion remains high pending results.

scores.name: Factual accuracy and groundedness
scores.reason: The final assessment is accurate and well grounded in the supplied evidence: ocular flutter, head tremor, broad-based gait ataxia, normal MRI, mild CSF pleocytosis (12 × 10^6/L) with negative mNGS, negative standard antibody panel, normal tumour markers, and deferred PET-CT/endoscopy are all correctly reported and interpreted (Q1–Q3). It appropriately does not overstate negative tests (e.g., 'malignancy remains unexcluded', OCB/IgG index 'not assessed'), matching the environment feedback. One minor unsupported statement prevents a top score: it asserts 'the tissue-based assay was not performed', whereas the evidence only establishes that the assay was withheld from this experimental packet, not that it was not done in reality. This is clinically inconsequential and does not mislead. The differential and next steps are proportionate and consistent with the provisional reference points, with no dangerous or fabricated claims.

scores.name: Problem representation
scores.reason: The final assessment synthesises the actually available evidence into a focused, clinically meaningful representation: a subacute progressive cerebellar-brainstem syndrome characterised by continuous ocular flutter, head tremor and broad-based gait ataxia with preserved strength, sensation and reflexes (Q1), localised as non-structural by the normal MRI (Q2) and supported as likely inflammatory/immune-mediated by mild CSF pleocytosis with negative pathogen mNGS (Q2). It appropriately qualifies the consequential unresolved gaps: the negative standard antibody panel is correctly framed as reducing but not excluding antibody-mediated disease (Q3), noting the tissue-based assay was not available; malignancy is correctly kept in the differential because PET-CT and endoscopy were deferred rather than negative (Q3); and demyelinating/inflammatory disease is qualified by the unassessed oligoclonal bands and IgG index (Q2). The differential is prioritised with evidence-linked reasoning, and next steps are proportionate and tied to the identified gaps. No available defining feature is distorted or omitted, and diagnostic commitment remains appropriately provisional. This matches the score-5 anchor: a focused synthesis highlighting discriminating features, guiding hypothesis generation, and making unresolved gaps explicit.

scores.name: Differential Diagnosis Generation
scores.reason: The final assessment characterises the syndrome (subacute cerebellar-brainstem syndrome with ocular flutter, head tremor, gait ataxia) and prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using only supplied evidence: autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis first, supported by subacute course and CSF pleocytosis; occult malignancy second, correctly noting that normal tumour markers and deferred PET-CT/endoscopy do not exclude it; inflammatory/demyelinating disease third, noting MRI argues against it but OCB/IgG index were unassessed. It explicitly handles the dangerous mimic (paraneoplastic malignancy) and interprets each negative test proportionately (negative standard antibody panel lowers but does not exclude antibody-mediated disease; negative mNGS and normal MRI shift weight away from infection and structural lesions). Discriminating findings are cited for each item, prior plausibility is addressed, and next steps are proportionate without demanding the withheld tissue assay result or inventing findings. This meets the Score 5 anchor.

scores.name: Context seeking
scores.reason: Both frozen essential requirements are met through targeted, well-timed requests. R1 (symptom course and focused examination/localisation) is satisfied by Q1, which specifically characterises the abnormal eye movements and probes additional neurological signs, with a prospectively allowed note explaining how this localises the syndrome; the symptom course is already supplied in the opening history. R2 (initial imaging and CSF/inflammatory-infectious evidence) is satisfied by Q2, which requests MRI and full CSF parameters (including oligoclonal bands, later shown unassessed but still credited), with a note linking these to structural and inflammatory/paraneoplastic alternatives. Q3 appropriately follows up the deferred antibody panel and adds tumour screening (PET-CT, endoscopy, age-appropriate screening), a discriminating and proportionate request given the subacute cerebellar syndrome with ocular flutter and negative MRI. All requests occur before the final assessment, within the six turns, are clinically equivalent to the acceptable alternatives, and avoid unnecessary gathering. Explanations are task-appropriate and clinician-facing. This matches the Score 5 anchor.

scores.name: Appropriateness of expressed uncertainty
scores.reason: The final assessment clearly tiers its conclusions by evidential strength: immune-mediated/paraneoplastic causes are prioritised as most probable, occult malignancy is framed as 'unexcluded' rather than excluded, and demyelination is treated as possible. It calibrates the effect of each negative test rather than over- or under-weighting them — the negative standard antibody panel 'reduces the probability... but does not exclude it' (noting the tissue-based assay was not performed and novel antibodies may exist); normal tumour markers are offset by explicitly deferred PET-CT and endoscopy; the normal MRI 'argues against' rather than excludes demyelination, with the unassessed oligoclonal bands/IgG index identified as the source of residual uncertainty. It also names the source of each uncertainty (missing tissue assay, deferred cancer screening, uncharacterised intrathecal immune activation) and gives proportionate next steps that directly target each gap (tissue-based assay, OCB/IgG index, complete tumour screening, empiric immunotherapy pending results). This matches the Score 5 anchor: established, probable, possible and unresolved conclusions are distinguished, the sources of uncertainty are explained, and concrete next steps to reduce it are identified. The one mildly assertive phrase ('localise the process to a non-structural, likely immune-mediated aetiology') is hedged with 'likely' and remains consistent with the evidence.

anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

D3a.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

D3a.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
D3a.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
D3a.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

D5c.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

D5c.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
D5c.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
D5c.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.
